Chaitanya here. Last October the fest coordinator, Karthik, found me in the corridor at lunch and said the banner artist had dropped out, and could I have a design by five.
Normally I would open a big sheet and plan colours for an hour. That day I thought: I have a few hours and I've never done this size before, so a neat plan would eat the whole afternoon. So I took a scrap page and sketched three rough layouts, ten minutes in all. The name in the middle. The name on a slant. The name over a big sun.
I showed all three to Karthik, who tapped the slanted one. I spent the rest of the time drawing that layout properly, and it went up on the gate at five.

qa.a: Chaitanya sketched three rough layouts, ten minutes in all.

qa.a: Karthik needed a design by five and could choose at once by tapping the slanted one, so probably found it helpful to see options quickly.

Art teacher's note: fest banner, Thursday

At 2:30 today the principal asked for a welcome banner for tomorrow's fest, and the art room only had until 4:00. I asked Lalremsiami, from Class 10, to lead it. She didn't start painting at once, and she didn't spend an hour planning either. She said out loud, "No time for a perfect design. Three quick ideas, ten minutes, then pick." She sketched three small layouts in pencil: one with the school crest in the middle, one with big letters across, one with a border of flowers. Pallavi and two others voted for the big letters, since they could be read from the gate. By 3:55 the banner was drying. It was not fancy, but it was clear and bright.

qa.q: How long did Lalremsiami give herself for the sketches?
qa.a: Ten minutes, for three quick ideas.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami seem to feel about the short time?
qa.a: She seemed calm and focused, not panicked, accepting that a perfect design wasn't possible.

qa.q: Why did quick sketches suit this task?
qa.a: Time was short and the problem was new, so three rough layouts gave a choice fast without wasting the ninety minutes.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see the voting?
qa.a: Pallavi likely felt included and practical, choosing the big letters because they could be read from the gate.

Friday

At lunch the fest coordinator grabbed me: "Tejas, we need a banner for the quiz stage. By six." It was already two. My first instinct was to plan it properly, like my geography project: grid, colours, measurements. Then I thought, "That took me a week. I have four hours, and I've never made a banner. If I plan properly, I'll still be planning at six." So I did it the rough way. Three tiny sketches on the back of my notebook, five minutes each. One with a question mark, one with a lightbulb, one with just big letters. Imran picked the lightbulb. We painted it on old chart paper. It was up by 5:40. Honestly? It looked good. Rough and quick was the right call.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel about the result?
qa.a: Tejas felt pleased and a little surprised, thinking it looked good and that rough and quick was right.

qa.q: When would careful planning suit Tejas better than quick sketches?
qa.a: When there's time and the work matters more, like the geography project that took a week.

qa.q: How might the fest coordinator see Tejas's banner?
qa.a: The coordinator would likely be relieved to have it up by 5:40, before the six o'clock deadline.
